summary: This article explains how the outer, middle, and inner ear work together to turn sound into something your brain can understand, and why loud noise can harm hearing.
introduce: Draw a simple cause → effect arrow on the board and ask students for an everyday example, such as “I did not sleep, so I felt tired.” Tell them that while reading “How Hearing Works” they will find at least two cause-and-effect links.

keyTerms.def: a thin, tightly stretched part inside the ear that vibrates when sound hits it
to shake very quickly back and forth
the small, spiral-shaped, fluid-filled part of the inner ear that turns vibrations into signals for the brain

challengeTerms.def: the formal name for the visible, flap-shaped outer part of the ear
relating to the eardrum, as in the tympanic membrane
relating to hearing or to the sense of sound

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that listening to loud music through headphones can damage your hearing? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain what happens to a vibration as it travels from the eardrum to the cochlea.
struggling: Read the first part of the article aloud together, review eardrum, vibrate, and cochlea, and let weak readers match cause cards to effect cards from the article with a partner.
gifted: Challenge advanced readers to use pinna, tympanic, and auditory in a short paragraph that explains one important cause-and-effect chain from the article.
